case_info.scenario: A 34-year-old previously healthy woman taking no medications was hospitalized after experiencing two 45-minute episodes of right-sided headaches over 72 hours, associated with transient left upper extremity hemiparesis and left hand numbness. She reported no smoking, drug misuse, alcohol consumption, or head trauma. Her mother and aunt experienced an ischemic stroke at ages 60 and 50 years, respectively. At presentation, her temperature was 36.5 °C (97.7 °F); heart rate, 70 beats/min; and blood pressure, 120/65 mm Hg in both arms. She had left-sided hemiparesis, with 4/5 strength in her left upper and lower extremities, and left-sided hyperreflexia. Findings on examination of her cranial nerves, sensory examination, and coordination testing were unremarkable. Complete blood cell count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, liver function test results, and C-reactive protein level were within reference ranges. Results of a urine cannabinoid screen were negative, and an electrocardiogram revealed normal sinus rhythm. A noncontrast brain computed tomography scan showed multiple right cortico-subcortical hypodensities, compatible with infarcts in the right junctional territories (border zone between the main cerebral arterial territories). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) confirmed subacute right frontoparietal infarcts on diffusion-weighted imaging and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery sequences. Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) revealed bilateral narrowing of the terminal portion of the intracranial carotid arteries, more severe on the right and with extension to the middle cerebral artery (MCA) (Figure 1).

case_info.explanation: B. Obtain digital subtraction angiography The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that a stroke in a young patient with bilateral narrowing of the terminal portion of the intracranial carotid arteries and a family history of stroke is highly suggestive of moyamoya disease. Intravenous heparin (choice A) is contraindicated because anticoagulation increases the risk of cerebral hemorrhage in patients with moyamoya disease. Lumbar puncture (choice C) is not recommended because there are no clinical signs of infection. Choice D is not indicated because steroids are not effective treatment for moyamoya disease. Moyamoya disease is a noninflammatory, nonatherosclerotic cerebrovascular disorder characterized by progressive stenosis of the terminal internal carotid artery (ICA), leading to fragile collateral vessel formation.1﻿Moyamoya(Japanese for “puff of smoke”) refers to the angiographic findings of this abnormal vascular network.2 Moyamoya disease occurs in 0.1 per 100 000 people worldwide, but the prevalence is substantially higher in East Asia, especially Japan (17.6 per 100 000).3Moyamoya disease is approximately 2-fold more common among females than males and has a bimodal age distribution (at 10 years and 30 to 50 years).4A family history of moyamoya disease is reported in 12% to 15% of patients with the disease.3 Underlying pathophysiological mechanisms are unknown but may involve alterations in genes involved in vascular development and angiogenesis, includingMMP,VEGF, andPDGFRB. TheRNF213p.R4810K gene variant increases the risk of moyamoya disease among East Asian patients.4 Patients with moyamoya disease may have intermittent transient ischemic attacks and strokes typically involving border zone areas or have hemorrhagic events (intracranial or intraventricular) due to rupture of fragile reticular vessels. Headaches affect 20% to 76.4% of patients, often with migraine-like features such as unilaterality and aura.5The differential diagnosis includes atherosclerotic cerebrovascular disease, autoimmune conditions (eg, systemic lupus erythematosus, antiphospholipid syndrome), and infectious vasculopathies (eg, meningitis, cytomegalovirus infection). The diagnosis of moyamoya disease is made based on digital subtraction angiographic findings of (1) stenosis or occlusion of arteries in the terminal portion of the intracranial ICA and (2) abnormal vascular networks in the vicinity of the stenotic lesions. Brain MRI or MRA are less accurate for diagnosis, particularly in patients with unilateral lesions, those older than 60 years, or those with early-stage moyamoya disease.6 There is no curative treatment for moyamoya disease. Among patients presenting with ischemic events, surgical revascularization with a direct bypass (extracranial-intracranial anastomosis) or indirect bypass (eg, placement of superficial temporal artery onto the brain surface to promote new blood vessel growth) is associated with decreased risk of ischemic stroke and death. Patients receiving nonsurgical management of ischemic events have recurrent annual stroke rates of 20% to 50%.7 Asymptomatic patients with moyamoya disease have a 1.4% to 15% annual risk of stroke.7,8For these patients, bypass surgery is associated with a 26% reduction in the risk of death but a 76% increase in the risk of hemorrhagic events compared with nonsurgical management.7 Per 2021 Japanese guidelines, based on limited evidence (grade C), antiplatelet therapy (aspirin, clopidogrel, or cilostazol) can be considered to reduce the risk of stroke in patients with moyamoya disease and a history of ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack, those awaiting surgery, or those ineligible for surgery due to advanced age or comorbidities.9Endovascular treatment (angioplasty and/or stent) is associated with restenosis rates of 68.8%, and high rates (9.5%) of complications such as vessel rupture and intracerebral hemorrhage.10 Digital subtraction angiography revealed an abnormal net-like vascular network with a “smoke puff” appearance near the stenotic terminal portion of the ICA bilaterally (Figure 2and video). The patient received aspirin (75 mg) and clopidogrel (75 mg). Seven days after initial presentation, she developed a new stroke and underwent an indirect bypass revascularization procedure. On postoperative day 21, she developed a right MCA ischemic stroke causing left hemiplegia. Two years later, she developed right-sided hemiparesis due to occlusion of the first segment of the left MCA and underwent direct bypass connecting the left superficial temporal artery to the left MCA. Four years after initial presentation, she has persistent left hemiparesis and a left steppage gait. Genetic testing revealed no pathogenic variants.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

Obtain digital subtraction angiography The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that a stroke in a young patient with bilateral narrowing of the terminal portion of the intracranial carotid arteries and a family history of stroke is highly suggestive of moyamoya disease. Intravenous heparin (choice A) is contraindicated because anticoagulation increases the risk of cerebral hemorrhage in patients with moyamoya disease. Lumbar puncture (choice C) is not recommended because there are no clinical signs of infection. Choice D is not indicated because steroids are not effective treatment for moyamoya disease. Moyamoya disease is a noninflammatory, nonatherosclerotic cerebrovascular disorder characterized by progressive stenosis of the terminal internal carotid artery (ICA), leading to fragile collateral vessel formation.1﻿Moyamoya(Japanese for “puff of smoke”) refers to the angiographic findings of this abnormal vascular network.2 Moyamoya disease occurs in 0.1 per 100 000 people worldwide, but the prevalence is substantially higher in East Asia, especially Japan (17.6 per 100 000).3Moyamoya disease is approximately 2-fold more common among females than males and has a bimodal age distribution (at 10 years and 30 to 50 years).4A family history of moyamoya disease is reported in 12% to 15% of patients with the disease.3 Underlying pathophysiological mechanisms are unknown but may involve alterations in genes involved in vascular development and angiogenesis, includingMMP,VEGF, andPDGFRB. TheRNF213p.R4810K gene variant increases the risk of moyamoya disease among East Asian patients.4 Patients with moyamoya disease may have intermittent transient ischemic attacks and strokes typically involving border zone areas or have hemorrhagic events (intracranial or intraventricular) due to rupture of fragile reticular vessels. Headaches affect 20% to 76.4% of patients, often with migraine-like features such as unilaterality and aura.5The differential diagnosis includes atherosclerotic cerebrovascular disease, autoimmune conditions (eg, systemic lupus erythematosus, antiphospholipid syndrome), and infectious vasculopathies (eg, meningitis, cytomegalovirus infection). The diagnosis of moyamoya disease is made based on digital subtraction angiographic findings of (1) stenosis or occlusion of arteries in the terminal portion of the intracranial ICA and (2) abnormal vascular networks in the vicinity of the stenotic lesions. Brain MRI or MRA are less accurate for diagnosis, particularly in patients with unilateral lesions, those older than 60 years, or those with early-stage moyamoya disease.6 There is no curative treatment for moyamoya disease. Among patients presenting with ischemic events, surgical revascularization with a direct bypass (extracranial-intracranial anastomosis) or indirect bypass (eg, placement of superficial temporal artery onto the brain surface to promote new blood vessel growth) is associated with decreased risk of ischemic stroke and death. Patients receiving nonsurgical management of ischemic events have recurrent annual stroke rates of 20% to 50%.7 Asymptomatic patients with moyamoya disease have a 1.4% to 15% annual risk of stroke.7,8For these patients, bypass surgery is associated with a 26% reduction in the risk of death but a 76% increase in the risk of hemorrhagic events compared with nonsurgical management.7 Per 2021 Japanese guidelines, based on limited evidence (grade C), antiplatelet therapy (aspirin, clopidogrel, or cilostazol) can be considered to reduce the risk of stroke in patients with moyamoya disease and a history of ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack, those awaiting surgery, or those ineligible for surgery due to advanced age or comorbidities.9Endovascular treatment (angioplasty and/or stent) is associated with restenosis rates of 68.8%, and high rates (9.5%) of complications such as vessel rupture and intracerebral hemorrhage.10 Digital subtraction angiography revealed an abnormal net-like vascular network with a “smoke puff” appearance near the stenotic terminal portion of the ICA bilaterally (Figure 2and video). The patient received aspirin (75 mg) and clopidogrel (75 mg). Seven days after initial presentation, she developed a new stroke and underwent an indirect bypass revascularization procedure. On postoperative day 21, she developed a right MCA ischemic stroke causing left hemiplegia. Two years later, she developed right-sided hemiparesis due to occlusion of the first segment of the left MCA and underwent direct bypass connecting the left superficial temporal artery to the left MCA. Four years after initial presentation, she has persistent left hemiparesis and a left steppage gait. Genetic testing revealed no pathogenic variants.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.explanation: B. Obtain digital subtraction angiography The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that a stroke in a young patient with bilateral narrowing of the terminal portion of the intracranial carotid arteries and a family history of stroke is highly suggestive of moyamoya disease. Intravenous heparin (choice A) is contraindicated because anticoagulation increases the risk of cerebral hemorrhage in patients with moyamoya disease. Lumbar puncture (choice C) is not recommended because there are no clinical signs of infection. Choice D is not indicated because steroids are not effective treatment for moyamoya disease. Moyamoya disease is a noninflammatory, nonatherosclerotic cerebrovascular disorder characterized by progressive stenosis of the terminal internal carotid artery (ICA), leading to fragile collateral vessel formation.1﻿Moyamoya(Japanese for “puff of smoke”) refers to the angiographic findings of this abnormal vascular network.2 Moyamoya disease occurs in 0.1 per 100 000 people worldwide, but the prevalence is substantially higher in East Asia, especially Japan (17.6 per 100 000).3Moyamoya disease is approximately 2-fold more common among females than males and has a bimodal age distribution (at 10 years and 30 to 50 years).4A family history of moyamoya disease is reported in 12% to 15% of patients with the disease.3 Underlying pathophysiological mechanisms are unknown but may involve alterations in genes involved in vascular development and angiogenesis, includingMMP,VEGF, andPDGFRB. TheRNF213p.R4810K gene variant increases the risk of moyamoya disease among East Asian patients.4 Patients with moyamoya disease may have intermittent transient ischemic attacks and strokes typically involving border zone areas or have hemorrhagic events (intracranial or intraventricular) due to rupture of fragile reticular vessels. Headaches affect 20% to 76.4% of patients, often with migraine-like features such as unilaterality and aura.5The differential diagnosis includes atherosclerotic cerebrovascular disease, autoimmune conditions (eg, systemic lupus erythematosus, antiphospholipid syndrome), and infectious vasculopathies (eg, meningitis, cytomegalovirus infection). The diagnosis of moyamoya disease is made based on digital subtraction angiographic findings of (1) stenosis or occlusion of arteries in the terminal portion of the intracranial ICA and (2) abnormal vascular networks in the vicinity of the stenotic lesions. Brain MRI or MRA are less accurate for diagnosis, particularly in patients with unilateral lesions, those older than 60 years, or those with early-stage moyamoya disease.6 There is no curative treatment for moyamoya disease. Among patients presenting with ischemic events, surgical revascularization with a direct bypass (extracranial-intracranial anastomosis) or indirect bypass (eg, placement of superficial temporal artery onto the brain surface to promote new blood vessel growth) is associated with decreased risk of ischemic stroke and death. Patients receiving nonsurgical management of ischemic events have recurrent annual stroke rates of 20% to 50%.7 Asymptomatic patients with moyamoya disease have a 1.4% to 15% annual risk of stroke.7,8For these patients, bypass surgery is associated with a 26% reduction in the risk of death but a 76% increase in the risk of hemorrhagic events compared with nonsurgical management.7 Per 2021 Japanese guidelines, based on limited evidence (grade C), antiplatelet therapy (aspirin, clopidogrel, or cilostazol) can be considered to reduce the risk of stroke in patients with moyamoya disease and a history of ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack, those awaiting surgery, or those ineligible for surgery due to advanced age or comorbidities.9Endovascular treatment (angioplasty and/or stent) is associated with restenosis rates of 68.8%, and high rates (9.5%) of complications such as vessel rupture and intracerebral hemorrhage.10 Digital subtraction angiography revealed an abnormal net-like vascular network with a “smoke puff” appearance near the stenotic terminal portion of the ICA bilaterally (Figure 2and video). The patient received aspirin (75 mg) and clopidogrel (75 mg). Seven days after initial presentation, she developed a new stroke and underwent an indirect bypass revascularization procedure. On postoperative day 21, she developed a right MCA ischemic stroke causing left hemiplegia. Two years later, she developed right-sided hemiparesis due to occlusion of the first segment of the left MCA and underwent direct bypass connecting the left superficial temporal artery to the left MCA. Four years after initial presentation, she has persistent left hemiparesis and a left steppage gait. Genetic testing revealed no pathogenic variants.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and

case_info.explanation: B. Obtain digital subtraction angiography The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that a stroke in a young patient with bilateral narrowing of the terminal portion of the intracranial carotid arteries and a family history of stroke is highly suggestive of moyamoya disease. Intravenous heparin (choice A) is contraindicated because anticoagulation increases the risk of cerebral hemorrhage in patients with moyamoya disease. Lumbar puncture (choice C) is not recommended because there are no clinical signs of infection. Choice D is not indicated because steroids are not effective treatment for moyamoya disease. Moyamoya disease is a noninflammatory, nonatherosclerotic cerebrovascular disorder characterized by progressive stenosis of the terminal internal carotid artery (ICA), leading to fragile collateral vessel formation.1﻿Moyamoya(Japanese for “puff of smoke”) refers to the angiographic findings of this abnormal vascular network.2 Moyamoya disease occurs in 0.1 per 100 000 people worldwide, but the prevalence is substantially higher in East Asia, especially Japan (17.6 per 100 000).3Moyamoya disease is approximately 2-fold more common among females than males and has a bimodal age distribution (at 10 years and 30 to 50 years).4A family history of moyamoya disease is reported in 12% to 15% of patients with the disease.3 Underlying pathophysiological mechanisms are unknown but may involve alterations in genes involved in vascular development and angiogenesis, includingMMP,VEGF, andPDGFRB. TheRNF213p.R4810K gene variant increases the risk of moyamoya disease among East Asian patients.4 Patients with moyamoya disease may have intermittent transient ischemic attacks and strokes typically involving border zone areas or have hemorrhagic events (intracranial or intraventricular) due to rupture of fragile reticular vessels. Headaches affect 20% to 76.4% of patients, often with migraine-like features such as unilaterality and aura.5The differential diagnosis includes atherosclerotic cerebrovascular disease, autoimmune conditions (eg, systemic lupus erythematosus, antiphospholipid syndrome), and infectious vasculopathies (eg, meningitis, cytomegalovirus infection). The diagnosis of moyamoya disease is made based on digital subtraction angiographic findings of (1) stenosis or occlusion of arteries in the terminal portion of the intracranial ICA and (2) abnormal vascular networks in the vicinity of the stenotic lesions. Brain MRI or MRA are less accurate for diagnosis, particularly in patients with unilateral lesions, those older than 60 years, or those with early-stage moyamoya disease.6 There is no curative treatment for moyamoya disease. Among patients presenting with ischemic events, surgical revascularization with a direct bypass (extracranial-intracranial anastomosis) or indirect bypass (eg, placement of superficial temporal artery onto the brain surface to promote new blood vessel growth) is associated with decreased risk of ischemic stroke and death. Patients receiving nonsurgical management of ischemic events have recurrent annual stroke rates of 20% to 50%.7 Asymptomatic patients with moyamoya disease have a 1.4% to 15% annual risk of stroke.7,8For these patients, bypass surgery is associated with a 26% reduction in the risk of death but a 76% increase in the risk of hemorrhagic events compared with nonsurgical management.7 Per 2021 Japanese guidelines, based on limited evidence (grade C), antiplatelet therapy (aspirin, clopidogrel, or cilostazol) can be considered to reduce the risk of stroke in patients with moyamoya disease and a history of ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack, those awaiting surgery, or those ineligible for surgery due to advanced age or comorbidities.9Endovascular treatment (angioplasty and/or stent) is associated with restenosis rates of 68.8%, and high rates (9.5%) of complications such as vessel rupture and intracerebral hemorrhage.10 Digital subtraction angiography revealed an abnormal net-like vascular network with a “smoke puff” appearance near the stenotic terminal portion of the ICA bilaterally (Figure 2and video). The patient received aspirin (75 mg) and clopidogrel (75 mg). Seven days after initial presentation, she developed a new stroke and underwent an indirect bypass revascularization procedure. On postoperative day 21, she developed a right MCA ischemic stroke causing left hemiplegia. Two years later, she developed right-sided hemiparesis due to occlusion of the first segment of the left MCA and underwent direct bypass connecting the left superficial temporal artery to the left MCA. Four years after initial presentation, she has persistent left hemiparesis and a left steppage gait. Genetic testing revealed no pathogenic variants.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },

  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."

case_info.explanation: B. Obtain digital subtraction angiography The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that a stroke in a young patient with bilateral narrowing of the terminal portion of the intracranial carotid arteries and a family history of stroke is highly suggestive of moyamoya disease. Intravenous heparin (choice A) is contraindicated because anticoagulation increases the risk of cerebral hemorrhage in patients with moyamoya disease. Lumbar puncture (choice C) is not recommended because there are no clinical signs of infection. Choice D is not indicated because steroids are not effective treatment for moyamoya disease. Moyamoya disease is a noninflammatory, nonatherosclerotic cerebrovascular disorder characterized by progressive stenosis of the terminal internal carotid artery (ICA), leading to fragile collateral vessel formation.1﻿Moyamoya(Japanese for “puff of smoke”) refers to the angiographic findings of this abnormal vascular network.2 Moyamoya disease occurs in 0.1 per 100 000 people worldwide, but the prevalence is substantially higher in East Asia, especially Japan (17.6 per 100 000).3Moyamoya disease is approximately 2-fold more common among females than males and has a bimodal age distribution (at 10 years and 30 to 50 years).4A family history of moyamoya disease is reported in 12% to 15% of patients with the disease.3 Underlying pathophysiological mechanisms are unknown but may involve alterations in genes involved in vascular development and angiogenesis, includingMMP,VEGF, andPDGFRB. TheRNF213p.R4810K gene variant increases the risk of moyamoya disease among East Asian patients.4 Patients with moyamoya disease may have intermittent transient ischemic attacks and strokes typically involving border zone areas or have hemorrhagic events (intracranial or intraventricular) due to rupture of fragile reticular vessels. Headaches affect 20% to 76.4% of patients, often with migraine-like features such as unilaterality and aura.5The differential diagnosis includes atherosclerotic cerebrovascular disease, autoimmune conditions (eg, systemic lupus erythematosus, antiphospholipid syndrome), and infectious vasculopathies (eg, meningitis, cytomegalovirus infection). The diagnosis of moyamoya disease is made based on digital subtraction angiographic findings of (1) stenosis or occlusion of arteries in the terminal portion of the intracranial ICA and (2) abnormal vascular networks in the vicinity of the stenotic lesions. Brain MRI or MRA are less accurate for diagnosis, particularly in patients with unilateral lesions, those older than 60 years, or those with early-stage moyamoya disease.6 There is no curative treatment for moyamoya disease. Among patients presenting with ischemic events, surgical revascularization with a direct bypass (extracranial-intracranial anastomosis) or indirect bypass (eg, placement of superficial temporal artery onto the brain surface to promote new blood vessel growth) is associated with decreased risk of ischemic stroke and death. You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.scenario: A 34-year-old previously healthy woman taking no medications was hospitalized after experiencing two 45-minute episodes of right-sided headaches over 72 hours, associated with transient left upper extremity hemiparesis and left hand numbness. She reported no smoking, drug misuse, alcohol consumption, or head trauma. Her mother and aunt experienced an ischemic stroke at ages 60 and 50 years, respectively. At presentation, her temperature was 36.5 °C (97.7 °F); heart rate, 70 beats/min; and blood pressure, 120/65 mm Hg in both arms. She had left-sided hemiparesis, with 4/5 strength in her left upper and lower extremities, and left-sided hyperreflexia. Findings on examination of her cranial nerves, sensory examination, and coordination testing were unremarkable. Complete blood cell count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, liver function test results, and C-reactive protein level were within reference ranges. Results of a urine cannabinoid screen were negative, and an electrocardiogram revealed normal sinus rhythm. A noncontrast brain computed tomography scan showed multiple right cortico-subcortical hypodensities, compatible with infarcts in the right junctional territories (border zone between the main cerebral arterial territories). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) confirmed subacute right frontoparietal infarcts on diffusion-weighted imaging and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery sequences. Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) revealed bilateral narrowing of the terminal portion of the intracranial carotid arteries, more severe on the right and with extension to the middle cerebral artery (MCA) (Figure 1).

B, Magnetic resonance angiography showed bilateral narrowing of the terminal intracranial carotid arteries (yellow arrowheads), with extension to the right middle cerebral artery (pink arrowhead).
case_info.explanation: B. Obtain digital subtraction angiography The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that a stroke in a young patient with bilateral narrowing of the terminal portion of the intracranial carotid arteries and a family history of stroke is highly suggestive of moyamoya disease. Intravenous heparin (choice A) is contraindicated because anticoagulation increases the risk of cerebral hemorrhage in patients with moyamoya disease. Lumbar puncture (choice C) is not recommended because there are no clinical signs of infection. Choice D is not indicated because steroids are not effective treatment for moyamoya disease. Moyamoya disease is a noninflammatory, nonatherosclerotic cerebrovascular disorder characterized by progressive stenosis of the terminal internal carotid artery (ICA), leading to fragile collateral vessel formation.1﻿Moyamoya(Japanese for “puff of smoke”) refers to the angiographic findings of this abnormal vascular network.2 Moyamoya disease occurs in 0.1 per 100 000 people worldwide, but the prevalence is substantially higher in East Asia, especially Japan (17.6 per 100 000).3Moyamoya disease is approximately 2-fold more common among females than males and has a bimodal age distribution (at 10 years and 30 to 50 years).4A family history of moyamoya disease is reported in 12% to 15% of patients with the disease.3 Underlying pathophysiological mechanisms are unknown but may involve alterations in genes involved in vascular development and angiogenesis, includingMMP,VEGF, andPDGFRB. TheRNF213p.R4810K gene variant increases the risk of moyamoya disease among East Asian patients.4 Patients with moyamoya disease may have intermittent transient ischemic attacks and strokes typically involving border zone areas or have hemorrhagic events (intracranial or intraventricular) due to rupture of fragile reticular vessels. Headaches affect 20% to 76.4% of patients, often with migraine-like features such as unilaterality and aura.5The differential diagnosis includes atherosclerotic cerebrovascular disease, autoimmune conditions (eg, systemic lupus erythematosus, antiphospholipid syndrome), and infectious vasculopathies (eg, meningitis, cytomegalovirus infection). The diagnosis of moyamoya disease is made based on digital subtraction angiographic findings of (1) stenosis or occlusion of arteries in the terminal portion of the intracranial ICA and (2) abnormal vascular networks in the vicinity of the stenotic lesions. Brain MRI or MRA are less accurate for diagnosis, particularly in patients with unilateral lesions, those older than 60 years, or those with early-stage moyamoya disease.6 There is no curative treatment for moyamoya disease. Among patients presenting with ischemic events, surgical revascularization with a direct bypass (extracranial-intracranial anastomosis) or indirect bypass (eg, placement of superficial temporal artery onto the brain surface to promote new blood vessel growth) is associated with decreased risk of ischemic stroke and death. Patients receiving nonsurgical management of ischemic events have recurrent annual stroke rates of 20% to 50%.7 Asymptomatic patients with moyamoya disease have a 1.4% to 15% annual risk of stroke.7,8For these patients, bypass surgery is associated with a 26% reduction in the risk of death but a 76% increase in the risk of hemorrhagic events compared with nonsurgical management.7 Per 2021 Japanese guidelines, based on limited evidence (grade C), antiplatelet therapy (aspirin, clopidogrel, or cilostazol) can be considered to reduce the risk of stroke in patients with moyamoya disease and a history of ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack, those awaiting surgery, or those ineligible for surgery due to advanced age or comorbidities.9Endovascular treatment (angioplasty and/or stent) is associated with restenosis rates of 68.8%, and high rates (9.5%) of complications such as vessel rupture and intracerebral hemorrhage.10 Digital subtraction angiography revealed an abnormal net-like vascular network with a “smoke puff” appearance near the stenotic terminal portion of the ICA bilaterally (Figure 2and video). The patient received aspirin (75 mg) and clopidogrel (75 mg). Seven days after initial presentation, she developed a new stroke and underwent an indirect bypass revascularization procedure. On postoperative day 21, she developed a right MCA ischemic stroke causing left hemiplegia. Two years later, she developed right-sided hemiparesis due to occlusion of the first segment of the left MCA and underwent direct bypass connecting the left superficial temporal artery to the left MCA. Four years after initial presentation, she has persistent left hemiparesis and a left steppage gait. Genetic testing revealed no pathogenic variants.
